::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the superb lyrebird of south-eastern Australia is one of the best [vocal mimics]{.hl} known. About 80% of a male's song is made of imitations of other species, mostly other birds, and the imitations are remarkably accurate.

_Sources: Wildlife Victoria; Dalziell et al. (2012), Animal Behaviour_
:::

## Who I am

I am Dr Massimiliano Canzi, Max for short.

. . .

I studied linguistics in Milan (BA), Manchester (MA) and York (MSc), and returned to Manchester for my PhD.

. . .

I work on how listeners perceive speech and how speakers produce it, mostly with experiments and quantitative methods. Forensic speech science is one of my interests.

## Who are you?

Tell us briefly:

- Your name and your programme
- How much phonetics you have done so far
- A forensic case involving speech or language that you have heard of, in the news, in a podcast or on TV
- One thing you would like to take away from this course

# The course

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` female superb lyrebirds also [sing]{.hl} and mimic, especially when defending their nests, when they imitate predators and alarm calls. Their songs were long overlooked: adult females look almost identical to young males, so singing females were easily taken for males.

_Source: Dalziell & Welbergen (2016), Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution_
:::

## The book

Leemann, A., Perkins, R., Sullivan Buker, G., & Foulkes, P. (2024). _An Introduction to Forensic Phonetics and Forensic Linguistics_. Routledge.

. . .

- Written by practitioners and researchers in both fields
- Real cases, exercises and suggestions for further reading in every chapter

The book has exercises in every chapter, and we do many of them together.

- Try each exercise before you read the solution

## Recording your voice {.smaller}

For the Praat practicals (sessions 9 and 10), each of you records yourself once in the LingLab booth, at any time before session 9. It takes about 15 minutes.

| Item | Content | File name |
|---|---|---|
| Word list | 19 words in the frame _Say \_\_\_ again_, read three times | `S07_words.wav` |
| Sentences A | three sentences, read normally | `S07_A.wav` |
| Sentences B | three other sentences, read normally | `S07_B.wav` |
| Disguise | sentences A again, in a disguised voice | `S07_A_disguise.wav` |

. . .

Use the ID you receive in place of S07, and upload the four files to the course folder.

## The word list

Read each word in the frame _Say \_\_\_ again_, for example _Say heed again_:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| heed | hid | head | had |
| hard | hod | hoard | hood |
| who'd | heard | hud | think |
| this | three | car | nurse |
| water | butter | little | |

. . .

Read the whole list three times, at your normal speed. The first eleven words differ only in the vowel; the others contain sounds that vary across accents of English.

## Sentences A and B {.smaller}

| Set A | Set B |
|---|---|
| The north wind blew hard across the dark water all night. | In the dark, the water looked cold and much deeper than it was. |
| My sister thinks the red car parked by the school is hers. | Nobody thinks a car like that belongs in such a quiet street. |
| We heard the news on the radio and called two friends at once. | They heard a loud noise and ran back to the house. |

. . .

Read each set at your normal speed, as one short text.

## The disguised reading

- Read set A once more, in a voice that you think would stop your classmates from recognising you. Choose your own strategy, for example a different pitch, a different accent, a creaky or nasal voice. Do not whisper: we need f0
- Write down your strategy on the form you receive, and do not tell your classmates

## What this course is, and is not

This course gives you a grounding in the methods and problems of forensic speech science, and can be a first step towards further study. Forensic phoneticians train for years, at postgraduate level and in forensic labs.

. . .

It does not qualify you to do casework, and the book's authors say the same about their book.

# Forensic phonetics and linguistics

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a lyrebird raised in captivity in New South Wales in the 1920s is said to have learnt [flute tunes]{.hl} and passed them on to wild lyrebirds after its release. Flute-like songs can still be heard there, but recordings made over 40 years suggest that the local song has stayed stable over that period.

_Sources: Powys, Taylor & Probets (2013), Environmental Humanities; Probets, Taylor & Powys (2020), Corella_
:::

## Two fields

- [Forensic phonetics]{.hl} deals with speech and voices as evidence: who is speaking and what was said, or whether a recording has been edited
- [Forensic linguistics]{.hl} deals with language as evidence, from the authorship of a text to the language of police interviews and courtrooms

. . .

Despite the names, few practitioners work in both. Most specialise further, so casework is often done by teams.

## Where the fields meet

- [Language analysis in the asylum procedure]{.hl} (LAAP): where does an asylum seeker's speech suggest they grew up? (session 7)
- Record keeping, report writing and acting as an expert witness: the same principles apply in both fields, and in all forensic sciences (session 8)

## You do it every day

When you answer the phone, you analyse the first few words, usually without noticing:

- Do I know this voice?
- Does it match the name on the screen?
- Roughly how old is the caller, and do they sound local?
- Do they sound calm?

. . .

Forensic phonetics asks similar questions, with systematic methods and an estimate of how reliable each answer is.

## An old idea: shibboleth

> And the Gileadites took the passages of Jordan before the Ephraimites: and it was so, that when those Ephraimites which were escaped said, Let me go over; that the men of Gilead said unto him, Art thou an Ephraimite? If he said, Nay; Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right.

_Judges 12:5–6, King James Bible_

. . .

A crude [speaker profile]{.hl}: /ʃ/ for Gileadites, /s/ for Ephraimites.

## A recent shibboleth

- In 2022, Ukrainians reportedly asked strangers to say [паляниця]{.hl} (_palianytsia_, a kind of bread) to unmask Russian saboteurs (Hyde, 2022)
- The word was believed to be hard to pronounce for speakers of Russian
- _Shibboleth_ itself is now an everyday word for any sign of group membership

## Discussion

Is the pronunciation of one word enough to tell where someone is from?

. . .

- What else could explain the "wrong" pronunciation?
- What if the speaker knows the test?
- What happens if the test gets it wrong?

. . .

No: a single word is not a sound basis for a legal decision, and the book makes the same point. Session 3 covers how profiling is actually done.

## No two samples are the same

```{r vowels-sim, fig.height = 4.4}
set.seed(27)
vowel_means <- tibble(
  vowel = c("FLEECE", "TRAP", "PALM"),
  f1 = c(290, 720, 640), f2 = c(2250, 1560, 1080)
)
sim_vowels <- function(speaker, recording, f1_shift, f2_shift, n = 15) {
  vowel_means |>
    mutate(data = map2(f1, f2, \(a, b) tibble(F1 = rnorm(n, a + f1_shift, a * 0.07),
                                             F2 = rnorm(n, b + f2_shift, b * 0.05)))) |>
    select(vowel, data) |>
    unnest(data) |>
    mutate(speaker = speaker, recording = recording)
}
vowels <- bind_rows(
  sim_vowels("Speaker A", "Speaker A, recording 1", 0, 0),
  sim_vowels("Speaker A", "Speaker A, recording 2", 15, -40),
  sim_vowels("Speaker B", "Speaker B", 50, 120)
)
ggplot(vowels, aes(F2, F1, colour = recording)) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = vowel_means, aes(f2, f1, label = vowel), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = mist, size = 5, nudge_y = -95) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = NULL)
```

Simulated vowels: the same speaker never says a vowel twice the same way, and different speakers overlap.

# Beware the CSI effect

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` lyrebirds are famous for imitating [chainsaws]{.hl} and other machines. But the well-known recordings come from captive birds, such as one at Adelaide Zoo: as of 2014, no recording was known of a wild lyrebird mimicking a mechanical sound.

_Source: Taylor (2014), The Conversation_
:::

## Forensic science on TV

- Experts collect samples, interview suspects and analyse everything, alone
- Results arrive in seconds, from impressive software
- Conclusions are a [match]{.hl} or a [mismatch]{.hl}, "with 99.4% certainty"
- A "voiceprint" on screen matches a stored sample perfectly

## Forensic science in reality

- Analyses take days
- Experts rarely, if ever, report "match" or "mismatch": there is almost always some doubt
- Objectivity and transparency matter more than speed
- No two samples of speech are ever identical, so there is no such thing as a voice "match"

## Even DNA is not a "match"

- A DNA sample from a crime scene is identical to the suspect's DNA
- This does not mean the suspect committed the crime: it means they could have
- So could everyone else who shares that profile, possibly thousands of people
- Other evidence, such as where the suspect was or a motive, is for the court to weigh

## Two propositions

The expert weighs the evidence under two competing [propositions]{.hl}:

- [Prosecution]{.hl}: the two samples come from the same source
- [Defence]{.hl}: the two samples come from different sources

. . .

The expert then asks how much more likely the evidence is under one proposition than under the other. More in sessions 4 and 8.

## Similar is not enough

```{r typicality, fig.height = 4.2}
f0_mean <- 115
f0_sd <- 20
cases <- tibble(case = c("Case 1", "Case 2"), offender = c(116, 72), suspect = c(118, 74))
share <- function(x) pnorm(x + 5, f0_mean, f0_sd) - pnorm(x - 5, f0_mean, f0_sd)
cases <- mutate(cases, share = share(offender))
curve_df <- tibble(f0 = seq(45, 185, by = 0.5), density = dnorm(f0, f0_mean, f0_sd))
ggplot(curve_df, aes(f0, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = dim_col) +
  geom_line(colour = muted, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(data = cases, aes(xintercept = offender, colour = case), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(data = cases, aes(xintercept = suspect, colour = case), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(data = cases, aes(x = offender, y = 0.0215, label = case, colour = case),
            size = 5.5, hjust = 1.15) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Case 1" = kingfisher, "Case 2" = hornbill)) +
  labs(x = "Mean F0 of the speaker (Hz)", y = "Speakers in the population") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

Simulated mean F0 of adult male speakers. Solid: offender. Dashed: suspect.

## Similar is not enough

In both cases, the offender and the suspect differ by only 2 Hz. But:

- Case 1: about [`r round(cases$share[1] * 100)`%]{.hl} of speakers have a mean F0 within 5 Hz of the offender's
- Case 2: only about [`r round(cases$share[2] * 100, 1)`%]{.hl} do

. . .

The 2 Hz difference is much stronger evidence in case 2, because so few speakers have such a low F0. How common a feature is in the population is called its [typicality]{.hl}.

## Discussion

A TV expert says: "The voices match, with 99.4% certainty."

- What could the 99.4% possibly mean, and what would you need to know to judge it?
- Who should decide whether the suspect is guilty?

# Working with forensic data

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` while courting, a male superb lyrebird imitates a whole [mobbing flock]{.hl}: the alarm calls of several species harassing a predator. He does it when a female tries to leave and during mating, although no predator is around: an acoustic illusion that may keep her from leaving.

_Source: Dalziell et al. (2021), Current Biology_
:::

## The material

- Forensic material ranges from the mundane (phone calls about bank transfers) to the distressing (threats, recordings of crimes)
- Practitioners describe three main strains: graphic content, pressure, and cases that touch on personal experience (Giménez, Elstein & Queralt, 2020)
- In this course we only work with the cases discussed in the book

## Offenders and victims

- Notorious offenders are widely remembered; their victims much less so
- In 2019, New Zealand's Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern refused to name the man who attacked two mosques in Christchurch
- Forensic analyses often focus on the person who produced the speech, often the offender: the book asks readers to keep the people harmed in view, and to choose their words with care

## Ethics

- Know the limits of your expertise and of your methods, and never comment beyond them
- Be objective: no conclusion stronger or weaker than the analysis supports
- The expert's duty is to the court, whichever side asked for the report
- The accused is presumed innocent: if the evidence leaves doubt, the court must know

## Further resources

- [IAFPA](https://www.iafpa.net/): the International Association for Forensic Phonetics and Acoustics
- [IAFLL](https://iafll.org/): the International Association for Forensic and Legal Linguistics
- _International Journal of Speech, Language and the Law_
- Nolan, McDougall & Hudson (eds.) (in press), _The Oxford Handbook of Forensic Phonetics_
- [Forensic Transcription Australia](https://forensictranscription.com.au/): Helen Fraser's site on transcripts of covert recordings

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Forensic phonetics treats [speech]{.hl} as evidence; forensic linguistics treats [language]{.hl} as evidence
- No two speech samples are identical, so experts weigh similarities and differences and do not declare a "match"
- [Similarity]{.hl} counts only together with typicality
- The expert assists the court, objectively, within the limits of their expertise
- Cases involve real people, victims included, so we describe them with care
:::
